slides.headline: The layout, in one sentence
slides.body: A good layout makes the rules of this chapter the path of least resistance: there's an obvious place for everything that belongs in Git and an ignored place for everything that does not.

slides.headline: The layout, in one sentence
slides.body: No single authoritative layout exists.
A picture helps. Think of three fences at increasing distance from the author.
The first fence is at the desk: the ignore file, the filter, the hook.
The second fence is at the gate of the branch: a required check in CI.
The third fence is at the door of the server: push protection and push rulesets.
Quick quiz. Which fence can the author not step over, and still acts before the bytes are stored on the server?
C. The author can step over A, and B runs after the push.
Where the picture breaks: fences are independent, and these shouldn't be.
And one sentence for the layout: rules first, files second.

slides.body: 🟢 SAFE: two commits. Predict: after *.ckpt is in the ignore file, what does git status say when the checkpoint is retrained?

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for. Every one of them is common.

items: Adding an ignore rule for a file that is already tracked. Root cause: the index decides what is tracked; ignore files only describe intentionally untracked files.
Believing git rm --cached shrinks the repository. Root cause: it changes the index and the next commit; the blob stays reachable in history and every clone still downloads it.

Treating the pre-commit hook as enforcement. Root cause: the hook is per-clone configuration that is not installed by cloning, is skipped by one flag, and never runs for commits made through another client.
Different rules in the hook and in CI. Root cause: two implementations of the same policy drift apart, so a commit passes one and fails the other.
Relying on CI to keep secrets out. Root cause: CI runs after the push, so the bytes are already on the server and the credential has to be rotated.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. A team starts a new retrieval project by copying an old repository and deleting what it doesn't need.
For the next project the lead builds the repository in the order of the history you saw.
The CI job is made a required check, and push protection is switched on for secrets, because CI comes too late for those.
Six months later the repository has had outputs stripped by the filter many times and has had the CI check fail three times, each time for a clone that had not been set up.
Your turn. Do Lab 33.1, "Build a professional AI project repository from an empty folder", in lab-manual/m33-ai-ml-workflows.md.

beats.text: The data rules use a pattern worth understanding. /data/** ignores everything below data/. !/data/**/ re-includes the directories, which is necessary because Git doesn't look inside an ignored directory, so no later rule could re-include a file in it. !/data/**/*.ref then re-includes the pointer files. beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for. Every one of them is common.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for. Every one of them is common.

beats.text: Adding an ignore rule for a file that is already tracked. Root cause: the index decides what is tracked; ignore files only describe intentionally untracked files.
beats.tele: Adding an ignore rule for a file that is already tracked. Root cause: the index decides what is tracked; ignore files only describe intentionally untracked files.

beats.text: Believing git rm --cached shrinks the repository. Root cause: it changes the index and the next commit; the blob stays reachable in history and every clone still downloads it.
beats.tele: Believing `git rm --cached` shrinks the repository. Root cause: it changes the index and the next commit; the blob stays reachable in history and every clone still downloads it.

beats.text: Treating the pre-commit hook as enforcement. Root cause: the hook is per-clone configuration that is not installed by cloning, is skipped by one flag, and never runs for commits made through another client.
beats.tele: Treating the pre-commit hook as enforcement. Root cause: the hook is per-clone configuration that is not installed by cloning, is skipped by one flag, and never runs for commits made through another client.

beats.text: Different rules in the hook and in CI. Root cause: two implementations of the same policy drift apart, so a commit passes one and fails the other.
beats.tele: Different rules in the hook and in CI. Root cause: two implementations of the same policy drift apart, so a commit passes one and fails the other.

beats.text: Relying on CI to keep secrets out. Root cause: CI runs after the push, so the bytes are already on the server and the credential has to be rotated.
beats.tele: Relying on CI to keep secrets out. Root cause: CI runs after the push, so the bytes are already on the server and the credential has to be rotated.
